About Event

​The AI Conference Hack Day is where 350 builders unite to do something that was impossible a year ago: build a working product — a real business — in a single day.

​This isn't a hackathon in the old sense. No throwaway demos, no clever prototypes that die the next day. The AI Conference Hack Day brings together 350 builders, engineers, product and business minds to ship something real. Something that runs. Something a customers will actually use — and maybe pay for before the day is out.

​For one day, the usual excuses disappear. You don't need a team of fifty. You don't need a year of runway. You don't need permission. What used to be a roadmap is now an afternoon. What used to be a funding round is now a focused day of work and the will to ship.

​That's not hype. It's where the frontier actually is right now.

​Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicts the first billion-dollar company with a single human employee will arrive as soon as 2026 —

​Every one of those companies has a day zero. This is where yours could begin.

​Here's how it works. You'll have a single day to take an idea from nothing to a working product. You'll build alongside the sharpest practitioners in applied AI — the engineers, ML leads, and founders who already live at the edge of what these tools can do. Mentors will be in the room. The energy will be unlike anything else at the conference. And at the end of the day, prizes go to the teams who didn't just build something interesting, but built something real.

​The top prize is the one that matters most. The best product team won't just take home recognition — they'll take the main stage at The AI Conference the very next day to pitch a panel of top venture capitalists. That's the kind of room most founders wait years to get into. You could earn your seat in twenty-four hours.

​This is the bet we're making: that the next great company won't be announced in a press release. It'll be built in a room full of people who decided not to wait. It'll start as a half-formed idea on Day ZERØ and walk out as something real.

​The era of the solo builder, the tiny team that punches a hundred times above its weight, the one-person company — it's not coming someday. It's starting now, and it's starting here.

​This is your shot.

​Don't miss it.

About Event

​What if you could see 10 AI tools in action, try them yourself, and use them to solve real problems — all in one session?

​Buildfest: Demos and Challenges is a demo day, hands-on event where sponsors will show you what their tools can do, and then give you a small challenge to solve.

​No long workshops. No hours of setup.

​You’ll see → try → build → solve.

​Whether you're a developer, student, founder, designer, researcher, or just curious about AI, you can jump in at your level.

​Event Format

​You’ll start with a set of 10 sample datasets covering different real-world problems. You can choose one of them to work with, or bring your own dataset and problem.

​PS: You can convert the pdf to excel through online convertor

​Pick a problem

​You can work on problems like: Build a system that creates study plans for students, Help shoppers find the right product based on their needs, Automate information extraction and processing from invoices, Build an AI travel planner, Summarize notes and extract important actions, Match candidates to jobs and help recruiters screen applications, Analyze restaurant data and identify inventory/demand problems, Build an AI system that answers common customer questions, Turn a simple idea into a structured content workflow, Find and evaluate promising problems and ideas or choose your own problem and build something that matters to you.

​How It Works

​Each sponsor will have a short demo + challenge.

​First, they'll show you their product in action and explain what it does, why it is useful, and how you can use it.

​Then you'll get a small challenge where you can try the tool yourself.

​You don't need to use every tool. Use whichever sponsor tools make sense for your problem — one, several, or all of them.

​The goal is to understand how each tool can be used and then combine the right tools to solve a problem.

​Demo Schedule

​4:30–4:35 PM — Physical AI Room @ Whitney Xiao
Opening and MC — welcome, event overview, and introduction to the demo session.

​4:35–4:40 PM — BuilderBase @ Sean Chiu
Demo how organizers can create better events using BuilderBase.

​4:40–4:50 PM — Tenki @ Colin Lowenburg
Demo how to run code and AI workloads reliably in sandboxes or cloud compute using runners.

​4:50–5:00 PM — Flatkey @ Sofia Kao
Demo how one API provides access to hundreds of AI models and compare models by results, speed, and cost.

​5:00–5:10 PM — FinChip @ Gary Yang
Demo how to give AI agents reusable skills so they can perform specific tasks more consistently.

​5:10–5:15 PM — Kylon @ Saurabh Khire
Demo how to turn a business process into an AI agent that understands requests, uses information, and takes action.

​5:15–5:25 PM — Ask the W @ Yezhisai Murugesan
Demo how to identify what is worth building with AI, where automation helps, and where human judgment is needed.

​5:25–5:35 PM — Rocket Ride @ Joe Maionchi
Demo how to build an AI/data pipeline directly in the IDE, from raw data through processing and AI calls to structured output.

​5:35–5:45 PM — Sartorial @ Sumit Jagdale
Demo how AI-powered product discovery can understand fit, color, material, reviews, images, and context to make better recommendations.

​5:45–5:55 PM — Wasmer @ Ayush Ojha
Demo how WebAssembly lets you package and run code across different environments without being tied to one specific environment.

​5:55–6:05 PM — PromptQL @ Jakob Prince
Demo how teams can collaborate with AI to turn questions and conversations into actionable results.

​6:05–6:15 PM — Unlimit @ Robin Meister
Demo how Unlimit connects global payments, financial accounts, and digital asset rails to enable seamless cross-border money movement.

​6:15–6:25 PM — Lore @ Kaia Colban
Demo how teams working in Claude, Codex, and Cowork can collaborate on work-in-progress, breaking down traditional silos and allowing people and agents to learn from each other.

​6:25–6:35 PM — Massive @ Jason Gellman
Demo how Massive provides web access through millions of volunteer devices across 195+ countries, enabling AI agents, models, and data pipelines to reach sites across the internet in real time and at scale.

​6:35–6:45 PM — Light Sage @ Sean Er
Demo how Light Sage helps companies optimize the agent experience of their APIs, CLIs, and MCPs through tracking, benchmarking, and improving how coding agents discover and use their tools.

​6:45–6:50 PM — Bridge US @ Vin Wanfan
Demo how Bridge US matches the right people at events.

​You Can Mix and Match Tools

​The challenges are not isolated.

​You can use one tool, several tools, or all of the sponsor tools to solve your problem.

​For example, you could:

​Choose a problem → use Ask the W to plan it → use Flatkey to choose a model → build a pipeline with Rocket Ride → create multiple agents with Kylon → do code review in Tenki → Run workload in wasmer.

​Or ignore that entire workflow and create your own.

​The point is to experiment and discover how different AI tools fit together.

​Sponsors

​Tenki

​Tenki provides sandbox environments, cloud compute, and runners for executing code and workloads. It gives builders a place to experiment, run, and scale their work.

​Rocket Ride

​Rocket Ride helps developers build AI and data pipelines directly in their IDE. It makes it easier to connect data, AI models, processing steps, and outputs into repeatable workflows.

​Flatkey

​Flatkey is a unified access layer for AI, connecting teams to 328+ official AI models through one API. It supports models from providers such as GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and more, with transparent pricing and automatic failover.

​FinChip

​FinChip provides agent skills that give AI agents reusable capabilities for performing specific tasks. Skills can help make agents more useful, structured, and consistent.

​Kylon

​Kylon helps you create AI agents that can run business processes. You can turn workflows into agents that understand tasks, use tools, and take actions.

​Ask the W

​Ask the W helps you figure out what is worth building with AI. It helps identify good ideas, tasks that can be handled by agents, places where human judgment is needed, and the next steps to take.

​Sartorial

​Sartorial helps make products more intelligently discoverable and recommendable. It adds context such as social proof, material, fit, color, promotions, image meaning, and brand-specific ranking judgment to product discovery.

​Wasmer

​Wasmer provides a way to execute WebAssembly universally. It helps developers package and run code across different environments in a portable and consistent way.

​PromptQL

​PromptQL is a multiplayer AI workspace with a built-in Wiki for AI-first teams. Think of it like Slack for teams working with AI — where conversations can turn into shared knowledge, decisions, and execution.

​Unlimit

​Unlimit is the global financial infrastructure for the borderless agentic economy. Designed to bridge the gap between fragmented local markets and the future of autonomous commerce, Unlimit provides the programmable operating layer for the world’s most ambitious businesses.

About Event
​TrueFoundry Agent Harness Hackathon

​AI agents are easy to prototype and much harder to run in production. Once an agent touches real users, tools, data, budgets, and internal systems, the work becomes less about a clever prompt and more about routing, permissions, tracing, retries, evals, guardrails, cost controls, and deployment.

​Join TrueFoundry and HackerSquad for a full-day Agent Harness hackathon focused on building production-minded agentic applications. The goal is simple: take an agent use case from idea or prototype toward something that can be observed, governed, evaluated, and operated.

​TrueFoundry's AI Gateway, Agent Gateway, and MCP Gateway will frame the day. Builders will work on practical agent harness patterns such as model routing, controlled tool access, MCP workflows, observability, eval loops, fallback behavior, budget controls, governance, and deployment paths.

​This is a technical builder event, not a passive product pitch. Bring a laptop, a strong use case, and a willingness to build under realistic production constraints.

​What You Can Build

​An agent workflow with model routing, retries, and fallback behavior

​A tool-using agent with controlled MCP or API access

​An observability layer for traces, tool calls, latency, usage, cost, and failures

​An eval or test harness for agent behavior across repeated runs

​A governance pattern for permissions, approvals, logging, blocking, or escalation

​A deployment-minded agent application that shows how it would run inside a real team or platform environment

​Why This Gets Hard in Production

​Agent systems need to coordinate models, tools, permissions, memory, context, retries, and fallbacks without becoming brittle one-off glue code.

​Teams need traces, audit logs, usage visibility, cost attribution, and eval loops so they can understand what an agent did, why it did it, and what changed between runs.

​Scaling agents means managing quotas, budgets, latency, provider failures, tool access, and security policies across teams.

​Guardrails need to become runtime controls: clear rules for what data an agent can see, which tools it can call, which actions require human approval, and how unsafe requests or outputs get blocked, logged, or escalated.

​Deployment gets harder when agents need to connect to internal systems, respect governance rules, and stay reliable as usage grows.

​Who Should Apply

​Platform, infrastructure, and backend engineers building or operating AI agent systems

​AI engineers and product engineers working with LLMs, tool calling, MCP, evals, or agent workflows

​Technical founders moving agent prototypes toward production

candidates.title: The Next Interface Hackathon: Rethink how we talk to AI
candidates.evidence:
The Next Interface Hackathon: Rethink how we talk to AI
For three years, using AI meant typing into a box and waiting for text to come back.
That era is ending. 

The next interface isn't a chat window. It's worn, spoken, and always on.
Glasses that listen.
A pendant that remembers. 
A tracker you never charge. 
A second self that watches your screen and acts before you ask.
We're putting the founders building that future in one room with the people who want to build on it.

Half a day in San Francisco. 

Real hardware on the table. Working demos, not slideware.
The lineup is a short list of founders shipping the wearables that are pulling AI off the screen. 

The founders in the room:
Adam Cohen Hillel, Secondly - a personal AI "second self" that sees your screen and acts across every app you use. The chat box becomes a presence.
Nik Shevchenko, Omi - the open-source AI wearable necklace, with 250+ developer apps already built on it. Always listening, always yours.
AnhPhu Nguyen, Mira - AI smart glasses with no camera. They hear what you hear, recall every name, and translate 60+ languages in under a second. AnhPhu is the Harvard builder behind last year's viral I-XRAY demo.
Andy Kong, Chargerless - a 7-gram health tracker powered by daylight. One minute of sun a day and it never needs a charger.
What you'll build: pick a device, an API, or a live sensor stream. 

Ship something a person could actually wear or talk to by the time we demo.

 The strongest builds demo to the founders in the room.
This is for builders, hardware hackers, AI engineers, and designers who think the keyboard is a temporary technology.

A twice-monthly working night for people building embodied AI. No robot required.
You built the arm at your kitchen table. You trained the policy overnight on your gaming rig. You collected the teleop data in your garage. The one thing none of it came with: labmates.
Degrees of Freedom is a monthly working night at Mission Robotics for everyone building physical AI without a lab around them. Bring the robot. Bring the sim that refuses to transfer. Bring the gripper that's been 80% assembled since the hackathon. For two hours, the people at the next bench are your labmates.
Schedule
6:00 - Kickoff: Who you are, what you're building, what you want working by 9pm.

6:30-8:30 - Bench time: two hours of real work, quiet enough to think, loud enough to ask the room when you're stuck.

8:30 - Demos: what moved, or put the problem that's blocking you in front of people who have likely fought it before.

Why come
The person next to you has probably already hit your bug. Robotics failure is multidisciplinary: the fix is rarely in the field you know best. A room of mixed builders is the fastest debugger in the city.

A stated goal and two protected hours move a project further than most weekends do.

A robotics space with a test area and workshop, open on a Tuesday night. The best place in San Francisco to set a robot on a table and work.

Bring anything with actuators, and plenty without: arms, drones, grippers, world models, sim pipelines, teleop rigs, half-trained policies, the URDF you can't get right.
